22 A microphone is connected to a cathode-ray oscilloscope (CRO). When a tuning fork is struck
and then held next to the microphone, the following waveform is shown on the display of the
CRO.
The time-base setting on the CRO is 2.00 ms per division.
What is the best estimate of the frequency of the sound produced by the tuning fork?
A
63 Hz
B
170 Hz
C
250 Hz
D
500 Hz

hints: Look along the horizontal time axis and count how many divisions are occupied by one complete sine wave from one rising zero-crossing to the next rising zero-crossing.
Use the time-base setting of $2.00\text{ ms}$ per division to convert that number of divisions into the period $T$ in $\text{ms}$, then in $\text{s}$.
Connect period to frequency with $f = 1/T$ and check that your $T$ of a few milliseconds gives a frequency of a few hundred hertz.
walkthrough: Identify one period on the CRO trace. One full oscillation is peak to peak or zero-crossing to the next identical zero-crossing. On the display each cycle spans $2$ horizontal divisions.
State the time-base rule: time = number of divisions $\times$ time per division. Here time per division is $2.00\text{ ms}$.
Calculate the period: $T = 2 \times 2.00\text{ ms} = 4.00\text{ ms} = 4.00 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}$.
Use $f = 1/T$ for the sound wave, since the microphone voltage follows the sound pressure variation. So $f = 1/(4.00 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}) = 250\text{ Hz}$.
A $250\text{ Hz}$ result matches a tuning-fork sound and the horizontal scale. This is option C.

A.explanation: About $63\text{ Hz}$ would need a period of about $16\text{ ms}$, which is the time for about four cycles on this trace, not one cycle.

B.explanation: About $170\text{ Hz}$ would need a period of about $6\text{ ms}$ or $3$ divisions, which overestimates the horizontal length of one sine wave.

C.explanation: One full cycle occupies $2$ divisions, so $T = 4.00\text{ ms}$ and $f = 1/T \approx 250\text{ Hz}$.

D.explanation: About $500\text{ Hz}$ would need a period of $2.00\text{ ms}$ or $1$ division, which is only half a cycle of the displayed sine wave.
